Promulgate

/PROM-uhl-gayt/ - the stress falls on PROM · verb

Hear It

What It Means

Promulgate means to officially proclaim or make widely known.

Universities promulgate their honor codes loudly during orientation week, printing them in every handbook and reading them aloud at convocation.

Worked Example

When the island nation adopted its first constitution, criers promulgated it the old way: read in full from every church step, printed on broadsheets, nailed to the harbor board — so that no fisherman could later claim the law was a secret.

Promulgate is official and outward-facing: an authority formally proclaims a law, doctrine or policy and puts it before the public. Announcing tells; promulgating tells with authority and on the record, which is why constitutions are promulgated while parties are merely announced.

How Promulgate Sits Among Its Neighbors

Synonyms — open each to see how it differs

proclaim

proclaim: to announce publicly and grandly; promulgate adds the official, legal weight

decree

decree: to order by authority — a decree commands, while promulgating spreads the word of it

Antonyms

bury

bury: to tuck something where no one will find it

hush

hush: to keep a matter quiet on purpose

How Strong Is It? — post → announce → promulgate

post vs. promulgate

post vs. promulgate: To post a notice is the minimum gesture — one sheet on one board; it stops far short of promulgate.

announce vs. promulgate

announce vs. promulgate: Announce goes further than post, actively telling an audience, but promulgate crowns the ladder: a formal, official proclamation pushed out until the whole public is presumed to know.

Sort It Out

Now place each word on the right side of promulgate.

Build the Word

The pieces

Prefix — pro

Prefix — pro: forward, out (Latin)

Root — mulg

Root — mulg: disputed - perhaps 'the common people,' perhaps 'to milk out'

Suffix — ate

Suffix — ate: to make, to do

Put it together

Put it together: Only the front of promulgate unfolds cleanly: pro- means 'out, forward.' What Latin promulgare's core once meant is genuinely disputed — 'bring out to the common people' and 'milk out into the open' both have defenders — so treat the rest as a single opaque piece. The sense, though, has been stable for two thousand years: to put a law formally before the public.

Why there's no relative to spot

Why there's no relative to spot: The pro- ('out, forward') is plain enough, but Romans left no clear record of what -mulgare meant: one guess connects it to vulgus, 'the common people,' another to mulgere, 'to milk out.' With the root's identity disputed, English has no safe relative to point to.

Strength Check

Word Choice

formal / official

Promulgate belongs to governments, courts and churches: laws, doctrines and regulations are promulgated. For everyday news, announce; for informal spreading, circulate — a word in this unit's reference list. If no authority stands behind the message, promulgate will sound comically grand.
